questions.knowledge_point: Visualizing Intersections of Uncountable Families of Indexed Sets
questions.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}={i}\times [0,{i}^{2}].$ Which of the following represents ${⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=1,$ we have

$$
{X}_{1}={1}\times [0,{1}^{2}]={(1,k)\,:\,k\in [0,1]}.
$$

This represents a vertical line segment from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(1,1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/6b6a47e464623fe9c572a52f7c71377136e68f41dcfd641920634b415568d7f5.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}={i}\times [0,{i}^{2}]={(i,{k}^{2})\,:\,k\in [0,i]}
$$

is the vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i,{i}^{2}).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/c67cd0b545f0fc779d2977e38fab8164eb3b0161a18e32a615c71d88d1c30b68.png)

There are no points that lie in all sets. Therefore, the intersection of the indexed sets is $∅,$ the empty set.

questions.knowledge_point: Sketching Cartesian Products of Special Sets in the Coordinate Plane
questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=N\times R$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=N\times R
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a natural number and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in N,\,y\in R}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{1}={(1,y)\,:\,y\in R}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/067b3b386273b09d5614f934f6525bd3e43ff46f420eb8aa7e744f635ff6d101.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number.

$$
{S}_{2}={(2,y)\,:\,y\in R}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/a870f65350ad00d258471079a34bec49a47d331c176dc7a91b3c7aae5ae968dd.png)

We can create the subsets ${S}_{3},{S}_{4},{S}_{5},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times N & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $R\times N$ as the set of vertical lines shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/c0df23ec47d729f597c02acff1530dd646a6f6c506a6497a8cb4d75b7fce5e74.png)

questions.problem: Which of the following represents the set $S=[-1,1]\times [0,1]$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B={(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S=[-1,1]\times [0,1]
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S={(x,y)\,:\,x\in [-1,1],\,y\in [0,1]}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{0}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $0$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
{S}_{0}={(0,y)\,:\,y\in [0,1]}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/1cc30fcc7543bfbbf8c5c59d1436eb3b1a0799d60c9ad1d899957e8fd17d58ab.png)

Now, consider a general ${S}_{i}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some $i\in [-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
{S}_{i}={(i,y)\,:\,y\in [0,1]}
$$

For each $i\in [-1,1],$ ${S}_{i}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/494c9d77b0ff339b90792270c9d641054a03a2918e3c56a93747b42a77ee3ccf.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $I=[-1,1]:$

$$
S={⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}.
$$

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following rectangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/7c5ac5dad0aaacb4347c260d634e6bcd2d6102b25d51813fe106803417cc7539.png)

questions.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[0,1]\times [0,i].$ Which of the following represents ${⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[0,1]\times [0,0.5]={(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,1],b\in [0,0.5]}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(0,1),$ $(0.5,1),$ and $(0.5,0)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/0fef44c4b8c4911a892d7dad4502edbb80ef236553d6fddb57de1472bd44a62b.png)

$$
{X}_{i}=[0,1]\times [0,i]={(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,1],b\in [0,i]}
$$

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(0,1),$ $(i,1),$ and $(i,0).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/f4602a46d3e4fc1799a475f05548ef278fdd33d354d1ec19ca4e5c5cc34cfcf8.png)

The intersection of all these rectangles is the line segments $[0,1]\times {0}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14094658/assets/19a2cd951a55508269a0034aec582345bf7e350ec516fe1eecac0d6bf5847981.png)
